title: The Dark Has Fallen Still, and All Night Your Heart Throbs
intro: Hafiz Ibrahim wrote this in 1325 AH (1908 CE) to congratulate Khedive Abbas II on Eid al-Adha and to thank him for pardoning the prisoners of Dinshaway, villagers tried after a clash with British officers in 1906, as the poem's heading and the notes in his Diwan say. The anthology Mukhtarat al-Zuhur records that Ismail Sabri had published a poem for the feast and the pardon, that Ahmad Shawqi wrote one on the same theme, and that Hafiz followed with this third; it answers Sabri's “If the ruins of the dwellings could speak” in the same metre and rhyme. It opens with twenty lines of love: on a sleepless night the poet reproaches himself for hiding his love and letting rhyme desert him, then answers that he is still in love, with a harsh beloved whose secret he has sworn to keep; he then turns to Sabri, whose poem has made it lawful for him to complain of love, and to Shawqi, and ends with praise of the Khedive and a line borrowed from Sabri, while the recitation gives the love prelude alone, nineteen of its twenty lines. Muhammad Rajab al-Bayyumi writes that readers took great delight in this exchange between Sabri, Shawqi and Hafiz.

translation: The dark has fallen still, and all night your heart throbs;
a care that gives no rest has set upon your sides.
1.sharh: On a sleepless night the poet speaks to himself. The night has gone quiet, but his heart has throbbed right through it, and a nagging care has fallen on him so that he cannot rest on either side.

translation: The bed is at a loss, and you are lost in it,
so under the dark the pair of you lie, tormented and sleepless.
2.sharh: Even the bed cannot settle him: it is at a loss as he tosses, and he is lost in it. Most likely the bed is the one tormented by his tossing and he the one kept awake, though either word fits both.

translation: Time has slipped by while you are spellbound by your hopes,
and youth has gone while you sit lost, head bowed.
3.sharh: The years have run on while he chased hopes he could not reach, and his youth has passed while he sat dreaming with his head down. Each half pairs time's passing with his own distraction.

translation: How strange that silence pleases you when you are in love,
while passion stirs others into speech.
4.sharh: He marvels at himself: he is in love and yet enjoys keeping quiet, while love moves other men to speak out in verse. This silence is the first thing he reproaches himself for.

translation: Passion was made for your heart and tongue, and yet
people have long doubted your heart and tongue, and gone too far.
5.sharh: His heart and tongue were made for love, one to feel it and one to voice it, yet people have long thought the worst of both, taking his heart for empty and his tongue for dumb.

translation: They charged you with having got over love; had they seen
what you fold within those ribs, they would have feared for you.
6.sharh: Because he says nothing, people think he has forgotten love. Had they seen what he hides inside him, they would have pitied him. To them his silence means he is cured; to him it is concealment.

translation: You have hidden your heart's secrets, but
a heart's secret is stolen from it by the eyes.
7.sharh: He has tried to keep his love secret, but the eyes give away what the heart hides, as the Diwan's editors explain. In Arabic sirr, a secret, chimes with yusraq, is stolen, as if the eye were a thief.

translation: By your Lord, ease your heart of its distress,
and have mercy on your insides, for they are tearing apart.
8.sharh: He begs himself, in God's name, to relieve his heart and to pity his aching insides, which are breaking under what they hold. The relief he urges is to speak his love in poetry, as others do.

translation: Tell us of the days of those who, by going far away,
heaped their cares upon you and went their separate ways.
9.sharh: He asks himself to tell his listeners about loved ones of old, who left and scattered and left all their cares gathered on him. The line sets their scattering against the gathering of their cares.

translation: Why have the rhymes disowned you, when in their slump
they found a market nowhere but in yours?
10.sharh: He wonders that the rhymes now disown him, when once, slighted everywhere else, they found buyers only with him. Poetry is pictured as merchandise, and in its slump his market alone would take it.

translation: Why does eloquence stand at a door that is not yours,
weeping, its sobs so hurried that it chokes?
11.sharh: Eloquence, too, now stands weeping at another man's door, choking on its sobs like a beggar who has lost his patron. Without him, the line implies, fine speech has nowhere to go.

translation: In love I am just as you would have me: I still
play, and make up verse as I go, and love.
12.sharh: Now he answers the voice that has been chiding him: in love he is just as it would have him, still playing, making verses on the spot and loving. He has not got over love, whatever people think, and from here the poem speaks as “I”.

translation: My spirit, for all the blows of fortune, is young;
my branch, for all disasters, is in leaf.
13.sharh: For all that fortune has done to him, his spirit is young and his branch still green, like a tree that has not withered. Hardship has not killed either love or poetry in him.

translation: The one who set sleeplessness upon my eyes
is hard on me, and my heart clings to him.
14.sharh: The one who keeps him from sleep is a beloved who treats him harshly, yet his heart clings to him. Arabic love poems often speak of the beloved as “he”, whoever the beloved is.

translation: I pledged to him I would never tell, and that pledge
will be undone only on the Day of Reckoning.
15.sharh: He has sworn to his beloved to keep their love secret, and that oath will be released only at the Resurrection. As the Diwan's editors explain, his secret will stay hidden until then.

translation: He has made me wretched, near me and far away,
and the brother of misery is led straight to misery.
16.sharh: Near or far, his beloved makes him miserable: near, by his harshness; far, by the longing. Then a bitter maxim: the man born to misery always finds his way to it, as if guided there.

translation: I have kept to all that might please him, because he rides
the back of opposition to the ways I make my own.
17.sharh: He keeps doing whatever might please his beloved, because the beloved goes out of his way to cross everything in his nature. So the Diwan's editors read it: one seeks to please, the other to oppose.

translation: From him I have borne what defeats the forbearance of the forbearing
and what even a fool would shy away from.
18.sharh: He has put up with things from his beloved that would wear out the most patient of men, things that even a fool, who weighs no consequences, would avoid. His patience outlasts the patient.

translation: I have taken to stringing pearls from his mouth's front teeth,
and hanging them as necklaces and collars on the oryx.
19.sharh: Out of his beloved's teeth, pearls to a poet, he makes verses and hangs them like necklaces on beautiful women, the oryx of Arabic verse. The verb nazama means both to string pearls and to compose poetry.

3.1.4-5.meaning: “Spellbound by hopes”: in the Diwan's gloss, hankering after what cannot be had.

5.1.3.head: أَصغَران
5.1.3.meaning: Asgharan, “the two smallest”: the heart and the tongue. An Arab proverb says “a man is his two smallest parts”.

6.1.1-2.meaning: “Pelted you with salwa”: accused you of having got over love. Salwa is the solace of forgetting.

7.2.4.head: النَّواظِر
7.2.4.meaning: Nawazir: eyes; a nazir is the pupil, with which one sees.

8.2.2.head: حَشى
8.2.2.meaning: Hasha: the inner parts below the diaphragm; here, his insides.

10.2.1.head: كَساد
10.2.1.meaning: Kasad: a slump, when goods find no buyers; the opposite of nafaq, the brisk sale in tanfuq at the end of the line.

11.1.2.head: البَيان
11.1.2.meaning: Bayan: eloquence, the art of saying clearly and well what one means.

12.1.2.head: هَمّ
12.1.2.meaning: “As your aim”: just as you intend. The Diwan's editors gloss hamm here as resolve and aim.

13.2.1.head: عود
13.2.1.meaning: Ud: the wood or branch of a tree; here, himself.

15.2.1-2.meaning: Yawm al-hisab, the Day of Reckoning: the Day of Judgement, a name the Quran gives it.

17.2.1-2.meaning: “The back of opposition”: opposition ridden like a mount. The Diwan's editors take it as a figure for quarrelling and estrangement.

19.1.4-5.meaning: Thanaya: the four front teeth; thaghr: the mouth.

19.2.3.meaning: Maha: oryx, wild cattle; the Diwan's editors take it here for women whose eyes are as beautiful as theirs.
